acbl17:388: Jason Wei's insight that "your ability to improve a system scales with how easily you can verify its outputs" has special meaning for agent reliability. Traditional software systems have clear correctness criteria (unit tests, integration tests); the challenge with agent systems is that judgment-type outputs ("is this answer useful?") have no ground truth, so they cannot be verified with traditional tests. Skillify's multi-layer verification system answers this: deterministic functions are verified with unit tests, real data with integration tests, judgment quality with LLM-as-judge, routing logic with resolver eval, and end-to-end with smoke tests. Every failure mode has a corresponding test layer—nothing is missed. The deeper implication of this design: when you can independently and repeatedly verify every capability of the agent, improvement becomes an engineering problem—you can measure, localize, fix, and measure again. You go from "it feels like the agent got better" to "this metric improved from X% to Y%."

hatebg:321: This loop works because it resolves a fundamental contradiction: the agent's reasoning ability is both the source of reliability problems and the solution to them. If you simply let the agent work on "vibes," it will reason on its own where determinism is needed (committing type-1 errors); if you over-constrain the agent, it loses the ability to use judgment for new problems. Skillify's bootstrap loop lets the model decide for itself "where determinism is needed," then hardens that decision into structural constraints. This means the system does not rely on prompts to "tell" the agent when to reason and when to use a script—instead, the agent uses its reasoning ability to write its own judgment criteria, then uses those criteria to constrain itself.
